hunts.label: Sunday, Nov 22
hunts.subtitle: Warm, cloudy, and a little damp: squirrels are not fans of wet tails, but they do like acorns.

rules.title: Sunday is not Saturday
items: **Hunter orange is required** while deer gun season is open (through Jan 1). Your deer is done, but other hunters are out. Bear season ends today, Nov 22.
**Stop by 9:30 am.** Sunday firearm hunting on private land ends then. Plan to be unloaded and out by 9:00.
**Migratory birds are closed on Sundays:** ducks, doves, rails, woodcock, snipe, and crow. None are in this plan.
Open today: gray and fox squirrel, rabbit, quail, raccoon, opossum.
rules.note: Confirm Sunday rules and seasons in the current NCWRC Regulations Digest before you go.

items: Walk-in (5:55 am): about **59F**. Mild for late November.
9 am: about **63F**. The day reaches about 70F, so cool any game fast.
Wind: **NNE 5 to 10 mph** (daily figure). Hourly wind and gusts were not available.
Sky and rain: cloudy. Rain showers are possible Saturday night, so leaves and ground may be wet. Rain chance for Sunday is about **24 percent**.
Sunrise about **6:51 am**. Legal light about **6:21 am** (sunrise minus 30 minutes). Both are calculated.
Moon: **waxing gibbous, about 96 percent**, full on Tuesday. Rise and set times were not available.
conditions.meaning: Assumption: a near-full moon and warm, cloudy air mean squirrels and rabbits fed late and may start slowly. Expect movement as the light comes up and again after any drizzle stops. Wet leaves are quiet underfoot, which helps a slow still-hunt.
conditions.hours_note: No hourly table was available this run. Figures above are daily and morning temperatures only.

in_season.tip: Cloudy and mild. Look for them after any drizzle stops.
Wet cover makes them sit tight. A slow walk and a kick-and-wait push.
No covey seen here yet. Bonus only.

in_season: Raccoon and opossum are open. Take only a sure, close shot.
Bear is open through today. You do not hunt it. Stay aware near the swamp.
Deer: tag filled for the season. Do not shoot a deer.

plan.title: Holly Wall Seat
plan.why: New spot: the **thickest stand of holly beside the main trail, about halfway from the yard to the Junction**. Sit against a pine trunk on the holly's **north side**, facing **north-northeast**. The wind blows from the NNE straight into your face, so your scent drifts back toward the yard, away from anything feeding ahead of you. Holly berries and the pines around it draw squirrels, and the dense holly shelters rabbits. The sun is low and behind your right shoulder, and the clouds soften it anyway. Every shot goes between NNW and ENE with a trunk or the ground behind. The yard and house are behind you, so never turn toward them with the gun.

steps.text: Leave the yard on the main trail, about 25 minutes before legal light. Red light only. Walk 20 steps, stop 10 seconds. Gun unloaded. Wear rain gear and orange.
Stop at the big holly stand halfway to the Junction. Sit against a pine on its north side, facing NNE. Load #4 with the plug in. Red light off.
Legal light. Stay still. Listen for gnawing, falling cone scales, and rustling in the leaves. Scan trunks 20 to 40 yards out, from NNW round to ENE.
Sunrise, hidden behind cloud. If it drizzles, stay put. Squirrels often move right after rain stops.
Seated hour done. Unload. Still-hunt slowly NNE along the main trail toward the Junction: 3 steps, stop, scan near, middle, far. Shots N and NE only.
At the Junction, turn onto the loop trail toward the feed bins. Look under the oaks for fresh hulls. Load #4 again only when the muzzle is pointed north.
Rabbit push in the thick edge north of the bins, heading north. Kick, wait 30 seconds. Shots N, NE, or W only.
Unload. Count shells. Walk back to the yard on the main trail, doing the land task.
Unloaded and out, well before the 9:30 hard stop. Cool any game right away, since the day reaches about 70F.

items: **In the gun: #4** (plug in). Squirrel and rabbit to 35 yards.
**Right pocket: #7.5** for a close rabbit or a quail flush.
**Slugs: zipped in a separate pocket.** Bear defense only.
**.22 LR (optional):** head shots on a squirrel only, with a trunk or the ground certain behind it.
Pack - GRAB: gun, phone, water bottle filled, tell someone your plan and return time.
Pack - CHARGE: headlamp and spare flashlight before bed.
Pack - RESTOCK after the hunt: water, coffee or tea, nibble, nitrile gloves, .22 LR count, fatwood.
warnings: Never shoot a deer with birdshot. Not with #4, not with #7.5.
Swap shells in the open with the muzzle north. Count every shell in and out.
Wet bark and leaves are slick. Unload before crossing logs, ditches, or the swamp edge.

animals.name: Gray squirrel and fox squirrel
paragraphs: The most common game here. Grays work oaks, hickories, pines, and holly. A fox squirrel may show in the pines.
Cloudy, damp air: expect a slow start, then movement once any drizzle stops.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #4 at 20 to 35 yards, head and neck on a trunk squirrel.
With the .22: head only, wood or ground behind.
After the shot, wait 10 minutes. Mark the fall against two trees.

details.title: Technique: after-rain watch
steps: Squirrels shelter in dens or thick pine boughs during rain.
When the drip slows, scan pine trunks and holly tops.
Wet squirrels look dark and sleek. Look for the tail outline.

after: Tip: falling cone scales or holly skins mean a squirrel is feeding right above you. Look up slowly.
Tip: wait for the squirrel to stop on a trunk, then shoot. Never shoot one moving against the sky.

animals.name: Rabbit
paragraphs: Cottontails sit tight in thick holly, briars, and brush around the loop edges and bins. Wet days keep them in cover.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #4 or #7.5 at 15 to 25 yards, head and front shoulders.
Shoot only with the ground behind the rabbit.
Never shoot toward the south line or the field SE.

details.title: Technique: slow edge walk
steps: Walk the cover edge into the wind, with the cover on your N or W side.
Take 3 steps, stop 10 seconds. Look for a hunched brown shape low in the cover.
A rabbit that holds is looking at you. Find the eye, check the backstop, then shoot.

after: Tip: look under low holly branches. Rabbits like the dry dirt there.

animals.name: Quail (bonus)
paragraphs: Northern bobwhite. No covey has been seen here, so this is a bonus, not the plan.
If one exists it holds in low thick cover next to open ground and flushes all at once.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #7.5 in the right pocket is the quail load. #4 works to 30 yards.
Pick ONE bird. Never shoot into the brown of the covey.
Shoot only birds flying N, W, or E. Let south-bound birds go.

details.title: Technique: after the flush
steps: Mark where single birds land.
Walk to within 20 yards of a landing mark and stop.
Singles hold tight and flush one at a time.

after: Tip: a wet morning keeps scent close to the ground. Birds sit tighter.

animals.name: Raccoon and opossum
paragraphs: Both feed at night near the swamp and the bins. At first light the last ones head to hollow trees or brush piles.

details.title: Shot and load
steps: #4 to the head at 20 yards or less.
Approach from behind. Opossums play dead, so check before you handle.
details.note: Wear gloves. Rabies is possible in raccoons.

after: Tip: wet mud shows a hand-like print. Five long toes means raccoon.

animals.name: Bear and bobcat
paragraphs: Awareness only. Bear season ends today, so you may hear other hunters. Give a bear space, talk out loud, and back away. Slugs are for defense only.

skill.title: Skinning and quartering squirrel and rabbit
skill.principle: Warm days spoil meat fast. Clean the animal within the hour, keep hair off the meat, and get it cold.

sections.title: Squirrel: cut and pull
steps: Wear nitrile gloves. Lay the squirrel on its belly.
Lift the skin at the middle of the back and cut a small slit across it.
Put two fingers into the slit, one each way, and pull the skin apart toward head and tail.
Cut off the head, tail, and all four feet.
Slit the belly, remove the insides, and rinse in cold water.

sections.title: Rabbit: peel
steps: Gloves on. Cut off the feet and head.
Pinch the skin at the belly, slit it, and peel it off toward the head and tail like a sock.
Open the belly and remove the insides.
Check the liver. Discard the rabbit if it has white spots.
Rinse and cool at once.

sections.title: Quarter and cool
steps: Cut off the front legs, then the hind legs at the hip joint.
Cut the saddle (back) away from the rib cage.
Put the pieces in a cooler on ice or in the refrigerator within the hour.
Bury scraps well away from the trails.

details.title: Why the liver check
paragraphs: Rabbits can carry tularemia. White or yellow spots on the liver are the warning. Gloves and a hot cook (well done) protect you.

skill.checkpoint: After you clean your first animal, send a note: with what you found and what was hard.

land.intro: Continuing Saturday: learn which trees feed the squirrels, now on a new part of the land.
steps: On the way to the Junction, look under the pines and hollies near your seat for cone scales, holly skins, and fresh bark scars.
Under the oaks on the loop, look for split hulls and bright cut nuts. Compare with what you saw Saturday near the bins.
Count the leaf nests (round clumps of leaves) in the trees along the way.
Pace from the Junction to the best feed tree.
Send what you find with a note: message, for example: note: 10 fresh hulls under the oak, 4 leaf nests, 120 paces from the Junction.

safety: NEVER shoot south. The house is SW and the field is SE: no-shoot directions.
Every shot today goes between NNW and ENE, with the ground or a trunk behind the animal. The yard is behind your seat.
Hunter orange hat and vest are required (Oct 17 to Jan 1). Deer gun season is still open for other hunters, and bear season ends today.
Hard stop: all hunting ends by 9:30 am on Sunday. Be unloaded and out by 9:00.
Wet leaves and bark are slick, and showers may return. Keep the gun's muzzle up and watch your footing.
Mornings start near 59F and reach the low 60s by 9. Wear layers you can open. Cool meat quickly on a 70F afternoon.
hunts.regs: Check seasons, bag limits, and Sunday rules in the current NCWRC Regulations Digest before you hunt.
